title: The King of the Golden Mountain
paragraphs: There was once a merchant who had one child, a son, so young he could barely run on his own. The merchant had two heavily loaded ships out at sea, with all his wealth aboard them, and he hoped to make great profits. Then news came that both ships were lost. From a rich man he suddenly became so poor that he had nothing left but one small plot of land. He often went there in the evening to walk and ease his mind a little of its troubles.

One day he was wandering along, lost in gloomy thought, brooding with little comfort on what he had been, what he was now, and what he was likely to become. All at once a little, rough-looking black dwarf stood in front of him. “Tell me, friend, why so sad?” he said to the merchant. “What weighs on you so deeply?” “I’d gladly tell you if you could help me,” said the merchant. “Who knows, I might,” said the little man. “Tell me what ails you, and perhaps you’ll find I can be of some use.” So the merchant told him how all his wealth had gone to the bottom of the sea, and how he had nothing left but that little plot of land. “Oh, don’t trouble yourself about that,” said the dwarf. “Just promise to bring me here, twelve years from now, whatever meets you first when you go home, and I’ll give you as much as you like.” The merchant thought this was no great thing to ask. It would most likely be his dog or his cat or some such creature, but he forgot his little boy Heinel. So he agreed to the bargain, and signed and sealed a bond promising to do as he was asked.

But as he came near home, his little boy was so glad to see him that he crept up behind him, grabbed hold of his legs, and looked up in his face, laughing. The father started, trembling with fear and horror, for he saw what he had bound himself to do. Still, since no gold had arrived, he comforted himself with the thought that the dwarf was only playing a joke on him, and that, in any case, when the money did come, he would see who brought it and refuse to accept it.

About a month later he went upstairs to a lumber room to look for some old iron to sell, so that he could raise a little money. There, instead of iron, he found a huge pile of gold lying on the floor. He was overjoyed at the sight, and forgetting all about his son, he went back into trade and became an even richer merchant than before.

Meanwhile little Heinel grew up, and as the twelve years drew to a close, the merchant began to remember his bond and grew sad and thoughtful, so that worry and sorrow showed on his face. One day the boy asked what was the matter, but for a long time his father would not say. At last he told him that, without realizing it, he had sold him for gold to a small, ugly, black dwarf, and that the twelve years were nearly up, when he must keep his word. Then Heinel said, “Father, don’t trouble yourself much about that. I’ll be too much for the little man.”

On the appointed day, father and son went out together to the agreed spot. The son drew a circle on the ground and had himself and his father stand in the middle of it. Before long the little black dwarf arrived. He circled round and round, but he could find no way in, and he either couldn’t or didn’t dare to leap across. Finally the boy spoke up. “Do you have something to say to us, my friend, or what is it you want?” Heinel, you see, had a friend in a kind fairy who was fond of him and had told him what to do, since she knew what good fortune lay ahead of him. “Have you brought me what you promised?” the dwarf asked the merchant. The old man kept silent, but Heinel asked again, “What do you want here?” The dwarf answered, “I’ve come to speak with your father, not with you.” “You have tricked and cheated my father,” said the son. “Give him back his bond right now.” “Gently, gently,” said the little old man. “Right is right. I paid my money, and your father took it and spent it, so be good enough to hand over what I paid it for.” “First you’ll need my consent,” said Heinel, “so please step in here and we’ll talk it over.” The old man grinned and bared his teeth, as though he’d have been delighted to get into the circle if he could. In the end, after a long discussion, they reached an agreement. Heinel consented that his father must give him up, and so far the dwarf got his way. But the fairy had told Heinel what fortune awaited him if he followed his own course, and he had no wish to be handed over to his hump-backed friend, who seemed so eager for his company.

To settle the matter with something like a draw, they agreed that Heinel would be put into an open boat lying on the shore close by, that his father would push him off with his own hand, and that he would be set adrift, left to the good or bad luck of wind and weather. Heinel said goodbye to his father and got into the boat. Before it had gone far, though, a wave hit it and it tipped, sinking low on one side. The merchant believed poor Heinel was lost and went home in deep sorrow, while the dwarf went off, thinking he had at least had his revenge.

The boat did not sink after all, because the good fairy looked after her friend and soon lifted it upright again, and it sailed on safely. The young man sat unharmed inside until at last the boat ran aground on an unknown land. As he leaped ashore, he saw a beautiful castle ahead of him, but it was empty and gloomy inside, for it was enchanted. “Here,” he said to himself, “I must find the prize the good fairy told me about.” So he searched the whole palace through once more, until at last he found a white snake coiled up on a cushion in one of the rooms.

Now, the white snake was an enchanted princess, and she was overjoyed to see him. “Have you finally come to set me free?” she said. “For twelve long years I have waited here for the fairy to bring you, as she promised, because only you can save me. Tonight twelve men will come. Their faces will be black and they will wear chain mail. They will ask what you are doing here, but give no answer. Let them do what they like, whether they beat you, whip you, pinch you, prick you or torture you, and bear it all. Only don’t speak a word, and at twelve o’clock they will have to leave. The second night twelve more will come, and the third night twenty-four, who will even cut off your head. But at the twelfth hour of that night their power will end, and I will be free. Then I will come and bring you the Water of Life, wash you with it, and restore you to life and health.” Everything happened just as she had said. Heinel endured it all and did not say a word, and on the third night the princess came and threw her arms around his neck and kissed him. Joy and gladness broke out all through the castle, the wedding was celebrated, and he was crowned king of the Golden Mountain.

They lived together very happily, and the queen had a son. Eight years went by like this, and then the king began to think of his father and to long to see him again. The queen was against his going. “I know well that misfortune will fall on us if you go,” she said. But he gave her no peace until she gave in. As he left, she gave him a wishing-ring and said, “Take this ring and put it on your finger. It will bring you whatever you wish for. Only promise me that you will never use it to bring me from here to your father’s house.” He promised to do as she asked, put the ring on his finger, and wished himself near the town where his father lived.

In a moment Heinel was standing at the town gates, but the guards wouldn’t let him in because his clothes were so strange. So he climbed a nearby hill where a shepherd lived, borrowed the man’s old smock, and walked into town unrecognized that way. When he reached his father’s house, he said he was the merchant’s son, but the merchant refused to believe it. He said he had only ever had one son, his poor Heinel, who he knew had died long ago. Since the man was dressed like a poor shepherd, the merchant wouldn’t even give him anything to eat. The king kept insisting that he was his son. “Is there no mark by which you would know me, if I really am your son?” he asked. “Yes,” said his mother, “our Heinel had a mark like a raspberry on his right arm.” Then he showed them the mark, and they knew he had told the truth.

Next he told them that he was king of the Golden Mountain, that he was married to a princess, and that they had a son seven years old. But the merchant said, “That can never be true. He must be a fine king indeed, going about in a shepherd’s smock!” This made the son angry, and forgetting his promise, he turned the ring and wished for his queen and son. In an instant they were standing in front of him. But the queen wept and said that he had broken his word and bad luck would follow. He did everything he could to comfort her, and in the end she seemed to calm down. She was not calm at all, however, and was only thinking about how to punish him.

One day he took her for a walk outside the town and showed her the place where the boat had been set adrift on the wide waters. Then he sat down and said, “I’m very tired. Sit beside me. I’ll rest my head in your lap and sleep for a while.” But as soon as he was asleep, she slipped the ring off his finger and crept quietly away, and she wished herself and her son back home in their own kingdom. When he woke up he found himself alone, and he saw that the ring was gone from his finger. “I can never go back to my father’s house,” he said. “They would call me a sorcerer. I will travel out into the world until I come to my kingdom again.”

With these words he set off and walked until he came to a hill where three giants were dividing their father’s belongings. When they saw him go by, they called out, “Little men have sharp wits. He can divide the goods between us.” There was a sword that cut off an enemy’s head whenever its wearer spoke the words “Heads off!”, a cloak that made its owner invisible or gave him any shape he liked, and a pair of boots that carried the wearer wherever he wished. Heinel said they must first let him try out these wonderful things, so that he would know how to put a value on them. They gave him the cloak, and he wished himself a fly, and in a moment he was a fly. “The cloak is fine,” he said. “Now give me the sword.” “No,” they said, “not unless you promise not to say ‘Heads off!’, because if you do, we are all dead men.” So they gave it to him, telling him to try it on a tree. Next he asked for the boots too, and the moment he had all three in his hands, he wished himself at the Golden Mountain, and there he was at once. And so the giants were left with no goods to divide or quarrel over.

As Heinel drew near his castle, he heard cheerful music, and the people nearby told him that his queen was about to marry another husband. So he wrapped his cloak around himself, walked through the castle hall, and stood beside the queen where no one could see him. Whenever food was placed on her plate, he took it away and ate it himself, and whenever a glass of wine was handed to her, he took it and drank it. So although they kept serving her meat and drink, her plate and cup were always empty.

At this, fear and remorse came over her. She went to her room alone and sat there weeping, and he followed her. “Alas!” she said to herself. “Was I not set free once? Then why does this enchantment still seem to hold me?”

“False and fickle one!” he said. “Yes, someone did come who set you free, and he is near you again now. But how have you treated him? Did he deserve such treatment from you?” Then he went out, sent the guests away, and declared the wedding over, because he had come back to his kingdom. But the princes, nobles and great men laughed at him. He would not argue with them, though, and simply asked whether they would leave in peace or not. At that they turned on him and tried to seize him, but he drew his sword. “Heads off!” he cried, and at the word the traitors’ heads fell at his feet, and Heinel was king of the Golden Mountain once more.
